questions.question: Compare test, exec, match and matchAll. When do you get capture groups, and when do you get all matches?
questions.answer:
test(str) returns a boolean and is the right choice for validation. exec(str) returns an array-like match object: index 0 is the full match, 1..n are capture groups, plus index, input and groups for named captures; it returns null when there is no match. With the g flag, exec resumes from lastIndex on each call, which lets you loop through matches but makes repeated exec calls stateful.

String.prototype.match is overloaded: without g it behaves like exec (one match with groups and index); with g it returns an array of full matched strings only, with no groups, indices or named captures. String.prototype.matchAll requires g and returns an iterator of full match objects, so it is the tool for extracting every occurrence with groups. test and exec live on the regex; match and matchAll live on the string. For a simple yes/no check use test without g; for all structured matches use matchAll with g.
key_points: test → boolean; exec → match object or null
With g, exec advances lastIndex
match with g loses groups and indices
matchAll needs g and yields full match objects

questions.answer:
The g flag makes test stateful. The first call starts at lastIndex 0, finds the lowercase a at index 3, and sets lastIndex to 4. The second call starts searching at index 4, which is the end of the 4-character string, so it finds nothing, returns false, and resets lastIndex to 0. A third call would return true again. The string looks identical each time, but the regex object carries state between calls.

This is why reusing a global regex for independent checks is dangerous: a validation function or render can return different answers depending on how many times it has run before. Fixes: use a non-global regex for test (/a/), reset re.lastIndex = 0 before each independent test, or create the regex inside the function. Do not share a /g regex across requests or components. Note the uppercase A is not matched because the regex has no i flag; the only match is the final lowercase a.
key_points: g makes test/exec advance lastIndex
LastIndex persists between calls
After a failed match, lastIndex resets to 0
Use a non-global regex for repeated validation

questions.question: What do these two lines print, and why? "Kakade".match(/<.+>/)[0] "Kakade".match(/<.+?>/)[0]
questions.answer: The first prints Kakade; the second prints . + is greedy by default, so .+ consumes as much as possible and then backtracks only enough to let the final > match. That final > is the closing tag, so the whole string is captured. Adding ? makes the quantifier lazy: .+? consumes as little as possible, so it stops at the first > it can use, which is the one ending . The same choice matters when extracting quoted values or a single attribute. Greedy is usually correct for validation, where you want the whole input consumed. Lazy is useful for pulling one field out of a larger string, but it is not an HTML parser: nested tags and > inside attributes still break both patterns. Use DOMParser or the DOM for real HTML.
key_points: Greedy + takes the most, then backtracks
Lazy +? takes the least
Neither parses nested HTML correctly
Choose based on whether you validate or extract

questions.question: Explain capturing groups, non-capturing groups, named groups and backreferences. How do replacement tokens differ from backreferences?
questions.answer:
A capturing group (pattern) saves the sub-match and numbers it left to right; m[1] is the first group, m[2] the second. A non-capturing group (?:pattern) groups for quantifiers or alternation without adding a capture number, which keeps numbering stable. A named group (?<name>pattern) is still a capture but is also available as m.groups.name and can be referenced inside the pattern as \k<name>. An unnamed group can be referenced inside the pattern as \1, \2 and so on.

Backreferences are pattern syntax: they require the same text to appear again, so /(\w+)\s+\1/ matches a repeated word. Replacement tokens are string syntax used by replace: $1 and $<name> insert captured text into the output, $& is the whole match, and $$ is a literal dollar. They look similar but run at different times: \1 constrains the match, $1 builds the result. Named groups make both directions more readable and survive refactoring better than counting parentheses.
key_points: (...) captures; (?:...) groups without capturing
(?<name>...) exposes m.groups.name
\1 and \k<name> are in-pattern backreferences
$1 and $<name> are replacement tokens

questions.answer:
The first pattern means digits not followed by a comma. On "20," the engine first tries \d+ = "20", sees the comma, and the negative lookahead fails. It then backtracks: \d+ = "2" leaves "0" next, which is not a comma, so the lookahead succeeds and the match is "2". The same happens to "40" -> "4". "60" is followed by end-of-string, so it matches fully. Result: [ '2', '4', '60' ].

The second pattern adds \b after \d+. A word boundary cannot sit between "2" and "0" because both are word characters, so backtracking to "2" is impossible. Only "60" satisfies the boundary and the lookahead, giving [ '60' ]. This is a general lesson: a negative lookahead after a greedy quantifier can be defeated by backtracking; anchor the token with \b, $, or a consuming class. Test the exact failing string, not just the happy path.
key_points: Greedy \d+ backtracks to satisfy a lookahead
\d+(?!,) can match the first digit of a number
\b prevents splitting a number
Lookaround is zero-width but still affected by backtracking

questions.question: What is ReDoS? Give a vulnerable pattern, explain why it explodes, and list practical defences.
questions.answer:
ReDoS (regular-expression denial of service) is a catastrophic slowdown caused by a pattern that explores exponentially many backtracking paths on a failing input. The classic is /^(a+)+$/ tested against a long string of a's followed by a character that cannot match, such as "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!". The inner (a+)+ can divide the same run of a's in exponentially many ways; when the final $ fails, the engine tries every division before giving up, freezing the main thread.

Defences: avoid nested quantifiers and ambiguous alternation such as (a|aa)+; make repetitions unambiguous by using a single quantifier over a well-defined class; anchor patterns; cap input length before testing (for example reject values over 254 characters); avoid running user-supplied patterns, and if you must, run them in a Worker with a timeout or use a linear-time engine. For validation, prefer simple negated classes like /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]{2,}$/ over clever nested patterns. A timeout cannot interrupt a synchronous regex on the main thread, which is why the length cap and input validation matter.
key_points: Nested/ambiguous quantifiers cause exponential backtracking
/^(a+)+$/ on a long failing input is the classic
Anchor, cap length, avoid nested quantifiers
A Worker or linear-time engine contains untrusted patterns
